extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, and NIH/staff interested in grant-funding disparities
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of how applicant characteristics (gender, race/ethnicity, degree, investigator experience, and submission behavior) relate to the probability of receiving an NIH R01 Type 1 award, using grant-management data and regression models. Focuses on whether a 'double bind' exists for women of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of receiving an R01 Type 1 award
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary outcome: the probability that an application (or applicant) receives an NIH R01 Type 1 award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured from NIH grants-management data (2000–2006) and, in some analyses, whether an applicant received at least one R01 award between 1980 and 2006. This is the dependent variable in descriptive statistics and probit models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant sex (female vs male) as a predictor of R01 award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses compare award probabilities by gender overall and within race/ethnicity groups; the paper reports that white women PhDs and MDs were as likely as white men to receive an R01 award, while women of color faced different outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race/ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant race/ethnicity (e.g., white, Asian, black) as a predictor of award probability and as an interaction term with gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings show that compared with white women, Asian and black women PhDs and black women MDs were significantly less likely to receive funding. Race/ethnicity differences are emphasized as explaining the funding gap for women of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree (PhD vs MD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of terminal degree (PhD or MD) held by the applicant, used to stratify analyses of award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper compares PhDs and MDs within gender and race/ethnicity groups (e.g., white women PhDs and MDs were as likely as white men to receive awards). Degree is treated as an important moderator of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator experience (new vs experienced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the applicant is a new investigator (those who had not previously received R01-equivalent funding) versus an experienced investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses present separate probabilities for new and experienced investigators (Figure 2). The paper reports that blacks and women who were new investigators were more likely to submit only one application between 2000 and 2006.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission behavior / number of applications submitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant submission patterns, including total number of applications and the likelihood of submitting only one application during the study period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women submitted fewer grant applications overall; the increased likelihood of submitting only one proposal is linked to lower award probabilities and is discussed in the context of competitive behavior (women avoiding competition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Race/ethnicity-specific gender differences (the 'double bind')
rubrics_metrics.description: The interaction effect evaluating whether women of color face compounding disadvantages (i.e., a 'double bind') relative to white women and men of any race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper explicitly examines gender differences within race/ethnicity groups to test for a double bind; conclusion: differences by race/ethnicity explain the NIH funding gap for women of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of descriptive statistics and probit models (methodological standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic approach: descriptive statistics combined with probit regression models to estimate relationships between predictors and award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models control for a large set of observable characteristics; methodological rigor includes appropriate specification (probit) for binary award outcome and stratified analyses by degree and investigator experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for observable applicant and application characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for covariates (a 'large set of observable characteristics') that could confound the relationship between demographic factors and award probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasize controlling for observable characteristics in regression models to isolate the effects of gender, race/ethnicity, degree, and experience on award probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication: diversity-focused interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that policies designed to address racial and ethnic diversity in the biomedical workforce may improve funding outcomes for women of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions link empirical findings to policy action: because race/ethnicity differences explain funding gaps for women of color, targeted diversity policies could ameliorate disparities; this serves as an evaluative consideration for programs aiming to reduce inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframe and data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of NIH Information for Management, Planning, Analysis, and Coordination grants management database for years 2000–2006 (and supplemental look-back to 1980–2006 for at-least-one-award analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying the data years and source is essential when evaluating or replicating the analyses; the new/experienced investigator classification and outcome windows depend on these timeframes.
